description: Full spanish team looking to "torear" this easy challenge.
summary: OliveTwin is an interactive web application that turns NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data into maps that show how agricultural land changes through the season, for any plot or area a user wants to study, or for two of them side by side. It follows the drying and recharge of surface soil moisture every 12 days with NISAR SME2, and adds NISAR backscatter (GCOV) and interferometric coherence (GUNW) to show changes in vegetation structure and field activity such as tillage or harvest. It combines these with optical vegetation indices, terrain, soil and climate data, and estimates how suitable the land is for crops such as olive, almond and rainfed wheat. Its Compare mode puts two areas next to each other and explains which one suits a crop better, and why. The processing pipelines only need the bounding box of an area. The live demo shows two example areas in Spain (Jaén and Toledo, June–October 2026, ~200 m grid). Radar observes day and night and through clouds. That lets farmers, cooperatives and agronomists follow the soil through a whole dry summer, at a time when climate change is making water the main limit on rainfed crops.
details:
What does it do?

OliveTwin builds a radar-based "digital twin" of any agricultural plot or area: the user defines its bounding box, the pipelines fetch and process all the data for it, and the web app lets you explore it or compare it with a second area. The live demo includes two example areas in Spain (Jaén and Toledo).

The app is a static website (no installation, no account) with four tabs:

  • Layers: shows any variable on the map with a timeline, legend and a short note on why it matters for the crop. Base maps: satellite orthophoto (PNOA), agricultural parcels (SIGPAC) or OpenStreetMap.
  • Analysis: studies one variable over time, with images by date, a change map, charts and statistics. When you pick a crop, it shows the crop's reference values (optimal, acceptable, unsuitable) and a crop-suitability map that tells which factor limits the crop and where.
  • Compare: picks Area A, Area B and a crop, and explains which area has more suitable agricultural land and why. It is useful, for example, to decide between two plots before planting or buying land.
  • Story: explains why radar matters and the hypotheses the app lets you explore.

Variables available for each area (in the demo: Jaén and Toledo):

  • NISAR radar (every 12 days, June–October 2026): surface soil moisture (SME2), HH and HV backscatter and the HV/HH ratio (GCOV), and 12-day interferometric coherence (GUNW).
  • Optical: NDVI and NDMI from Sentinel-2.
  • Terrain: elevation and slope from Copernicus DEM.
  • Soil: clay, sand, organic carbon and pH (0–30 cm) from SoilGrids.
  • Climate: 1991–2020 normals (rainfall, mean temperature, coldest-month minimum, annual absolute minimum) and daily weather for the season, including rainfall and reference evapotranspiration (ET0).
  • Land cover: agricultural land and olive groves from CORINE.
  • Reference soil moisture: NASA SMAP, as a regional check against NISAR.

How does it work?

  1. Data pipelines (Python) take the bounding box of any area and download real, open data for it from NASA Earthdata (CMR search, Harmony subsetting, earthaccess partial reads), Microsoft Planetary Computer, ISRIC, Open-Meteo and the EEA.
  2. All variables are reprojected and aggregated onto one common ~200 m grid per area, so they can be compared cell by cell. NISAR soil moisture uses nearest-neighbour resampling, so no values are invented, and a quality-filtered version uses the product's own retrieval-quality flag. Radar backscatter is averaged in linear power before converting to dB. Sentinel-2 uses the scene classification to mask clouds and shadows. Climate normals are interpolated between 5 points and corrected for altitude (6.5 °C/km).
  3. Crop suitability gives each factor a score from 0 to 1 against published crop requirements: climate (FAO GAEZ v4 for olive and wheat, FAO ECOCROP for almond), soil pH, texture, slope and organic carbon (University of Granada land-evaluation tables), and maximum altitude. Suitability is the worst factor (law of the minimum), classified as S1, S2, S3 or N. Compare only counts agricultural land.
  4. The results are published as lightweight PNG and JSON files, validated against a JSON Schema data contract, with full provenance: scene ID, acquisition date, processing version and licence.
  5. The web app (Vue 3 + TypeScript + Leaflet) reads those files directly in the browser. A CI check (data validation, tests and build) runs on every change, and GitHub Pages publishes the site.
  6. Optional AI interpretation: the "Interpret with AI" button sends the computed statistics to a language model that the user chooses. By default it is Gemma 3 (4B) running locally with Ollama, so no data leaves the computer. The model then explains the results in plain words. It does not take part in any calculation, and its instructions forbid inventing figures.

What benefits does it have?

  • Radar sees what optical satellites miss: day and night, through clouds, and sensitive to water in the soil.
  • One place, one grid: radar, vegetation, soil, terrain and climate side by side, comparable cell by cell.
  • Explainable: every map says where it comes from, and the suitability map shows which factor limits the crop.
  • Works anywhere NISAR observes: any plot, farm or region, defined just by its bounding box; and any two of them can be compared.
  • Free and lightweight: open data and a static website, so it is cheap to host and easy to extend to new areas.

What do you hope to achieve?

We want to give growers and agronomists a simple way to see how their own plots behave through the dry season, which crops fit them, and how two plots compare. As NISAR products become calibrated and longer time series appear, we hope to let users draw their plot directly in the app, add more crops, validate it with in-situ soil-moisture sensors and real yields together with growers and research groups, and eventually combine moisture, weather and crop needs into water-management guidance.

Limitations (stated in the app)

  • NISAR SME2, GCOV and GUNW are PROVISIONAL products (not fully calibrated), so we use them for relative changes.
  • Surface soil moisture covers only the top ~5 cm and is not an irrigation requirement.
  • Suitability is a physical land model; it is not a yield forecast and has not been validated against yields.
  • Adding a new area currently means running the pipelines for its bounding box. In the demo, Jaén is observed at dawn and Toledo at dusk. NISAR has gaps over urban areas, water and dense vegetation.

Tools, coding languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: TypeScript, Python 3.12, HTML/CSS.
  • Web: Vue 3, Vite, Leaflet, Ajv (JSON Schema validation), Vitest.
  • Data processing: numpy, rasterio, pyproj, h5py, shapely, pillow, requests, jsonschema, pytest.
  • NASA tools: earthaccess, harmony-py (NASA Harmony), NASA CMR.
  • Infrastructure: GitHub, GitHub Actions (CI) and GitHub Pages.
  • Optional AI: Ollama with Gemma 3 4B (local), or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
  • Hardware: standard laptops; no special hardware.

Use of AI in development (disclosure)

Part of the code, tests and documentation was written with AI coding assistants (Anthropic Claude and GitHub Copilot) under the team's direction and review. Those commits carry a "Co-authored-by" trailer in the public Git history. All data are real downloads from the cited sources, not AI-generated.
